quiz.where: ## Final test, sequence-reading-a-miss, "Which order of fixes is right?" (lines 409-419)
quiz.problem: Two of the feedback lines rest on a cost ranking the Lesson never teaches: (a) "it's the priciest change, so it comes last" and (d) "a cheaper effort change comes before a bigger model". The cited Anthropic guide doesn't rank them that way, and says a larger model can lower total cost on hard multi-step tasks. The question also asks for an "order of fixes", but you don't try fixes one after another. You ask diagnostic questions in order. And it repeats the flow Scene almost word for word, so it tests recall, not transfer.
quiz.evidence: https://claude.com/blog/claude-model-and-effort-level-in-claude-code (2026-07-07): check your context first, then ask whether Claude "did not try hard enough, or did it not know enough?". It never says effort is cheaper, and it notes larger models cost more per token but can lower total cost on hard tasks. Lesson flow Scene, lines 124-144.
quiz.fix:
```test sequence-reading-a-miss
Claude's fix to a book club's RSVP form came back wrong. Before you touch a dial, you ask three questions in turn. Which order lets each answer point to the right fix?
- [ ] Did it try hard enough? → Was the task clear? → Is the model capable enough?
  > If the task was vague, more effort just digs harder in the wrong place. Check the task first.
- [ ] Is the model capable enough? → Did it try hard enough? → Was the task clear?
  > You can't call it the model's ceiling until you know it had what it needed and did the work.
- [x] Was the task clear? → Did it try hard enough? → Is the model capable enough?
  > Right. Fix a vague task first, then check it did the work. Only a clear task, fully worked and still wrong, points to a bigger model.
- [ ] Was the task clear? → Is the model capable enough? → Did it try hard enough?
  > You only reach the model's ceiling once you know it did the work. A skipped file or test points to effort first.
```
